item.title: Middle Childhood Asks Something of Parents, Too
item.description:
Child Development

Middle Childhood Asks Something of Parents, Too

As our kids work out who they are, parents do the same.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Attachment shifts from physical closeness to the confidence that parents remain available when needed.
  • Middle childhood brings new self-evaluations as children compare abilities across social and academic domains.
  • Research shows that children’s independence reshapes how parents understand their role.

Last week, I dropped my youngest off at her first-grade classroom for her first day. She bounced into the classroom, excited to see her friends and meet her new teachers. She gave me a quick hug goodbye and was off.

This first day of school felt very different from the last few, when she begged me to stay and would only shyly approach her classmates while holding my hand. Here we were at middle childhood. She now had a sense of identity as a student and a friend, and not just a child.

I also had a slightly different sense of identity; the physical demands of parenting had lightened a bit, and the emotional demands, though still present, had changed. I had more time to myself and a greater need to feel secure in my identity as a parent and a person as I supported one of her key developmental needs of this period—finding her sense of self.

When attachment changes shape

It's easy to assume the quick hug is a sign that she needs me less. The research suggests otherwise. She just needs me differently.

In infancy and early childhood, the attachment system is organized around physical proximity. By middle childhood, the goal shifts from proximity to availability—the child's confidence that the caregiver can be reached and will respond if needed (Bowlby, 1988; Kerns & Abtahi, 2017).

This is partly a story about growing self-regulation. Children this age simply require less moment-to-moment assistance. But the need for an attachment figure has not diminished. It has changed shape—from a need for immediate in-the-moment support to her working model of whether I am reliably there for her, emotionally and psychologically.

Still, parents remain children's primary attachment figures through middle childhood. When asked whom they would turn to in situations that activate attachment needs, like feeling worried about a first day of school or who they would want to call after going away for two weeks at summer camp, even 11- and 12-year-olds show a clear preference for parents over peers (Seibert & Kerns, 2009). The widening social world does not displace us; it sits alongside us.

Further, the relationship increasingly operates as a collaborative alliance. The child is still relying on a stronger, wiser figure, but is beginning to use the parent as a resource rather than as someone who solves the problem outright (Kerns & Abtahi, 2017). Parents continue to serve as both a safe haven in distress and a secure base for exploration, and it is the secure base function that does the heavy lifting now, supporting a child's willingness to attempt hard things and to risk failing at them.

What she is working on

The identity work of this period follows a pattern. In early childhood, self-descriptions tend to be global (seeing themselves in the same way across settings) and optimistic. In middle childhood, children begin to evaluate themselves separately across domains—scholastic competence, athletic competence, social acceptance, physical appearance, behavioral conduct—and, for the first time, to form a sense of their overall worth as a person that they can verbalize (Harter, 2012).

What makes this possible at this stage in development is social comparison. Children this age can hold their own performance and a peer's in mind at once and draw a conclusion about themselves from the difference. That capacity is a genuine cognitive achievement. Once children can rank themselves, most of them will find themselves falling short somewhere, and domain-specific self-evaluations tend to become less rosy across middle and later childhood (Harter, 2012). So when my daughter announces that she is a fast runner but not a good drawer, she is not fishing for reassurance. She is figuring out who she is.

Galinsky's interpretive stage

Ellen Galinsky's The Six Stages of Parenthood (1987) remains one of the few frameworks that treats parents as developing people rather than just as the environment in which a child develops. Drawing on Erikson (1963) and Levinson (1978) and on interviews with hundreds of parents, she argued that parenthood reorganizes itself as children grow, and that each reorganization asks something new of us.

The stage that corresponds to middle childhood she called the interpretive stage. The tasks involved with this stage are recognizable to anyone living it. It involves interpreting the world to our children, deciding how involved to be, and managing the twin pulls of separating and connecting. But the task Galinsky lists first is the one I keep returning to—interpreting oneself as a parent. This is the period when our children ask us to articulate, often for the first time, what we actually believe about achievement, friendship, fairness, and effort. Our children are out experiencing the world for themselves and observing whether our answers hold.

Our own middle

Middle childhood for our children frequently overlaps with midlife for us. Midlife is characterized by a dense interplay of multiple roles—work, aging parents, children, one's own health—negotiated alongside the physical and psychological changes of aging (Lachman, 2004). The popular image is of crisis; the research is considerably more mixed and points toward peak functioning, a sense of control, and generativity. In Erikson's (1963) terms, the central task is generativity versus stagnation: investing in what will outlast us. Parenting a school-age child is, on its face, generative work. But the hours that open up when a child no longer requires constant physical tending are real hours, and what fills them matters. This is where the two developmental stories meet.

Why our identity matters for theirs

There is a reasonable intuition that parents who feel settled in themselves parent better, and there is evidence behind it. Parental self-efficacy—a parent's appraisal of their own competence in the role—is robustly linked to parenting competence, and to children's adjustment both directly and indirectly through parenting practices (Jones & Prinz, 2005).

Research on self-determination theory explains how our identity is tied to our children’s. For example, in a study of 154 mothers and their two elementary school-age children, mothers who reported greater satisfaction of their own psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness were perceived by their children as more autonomy-supportive. Autonomy-supportive parenting, in turn, was related to the children's own need satisfaction and to a more autonomy-supportive style between the siblings themselves (van der Kaap-Deeder et al., 2015).

This is the part I find most useful and most demanding. Supporting a child's emerging autonomy requires a kind of steadiness: the capacity to take her perspective, to let her try the thing badly, to hear that she is not the best reader in her class without rushing in to manage my own discomfort about it. That steadiness is easier to summon from a self that is not entirely staked on her performance. Galinsky heard this from parents four decades ago—that a parent's worth cannot rest on how the child performs.

The hug at the door

She was off in under 10 seconds, which I have decided to read as a good sign—evidence that she trusts I will be there at 3:00, which is precisely what availability is supposed to look like at six. What I did not anticipate is that her developmental growth would hand me a task of my own. She is figuring out who she is. So, it turns out, am I. The reassuring finding from decades of middle childhood research is that our tasks don’t need to compete. Together, our identities will grow and adapt alongside one another.

item.title: How Self-Compassion Changes the Way We Experience Failure
item.description:
Self-Talk

How Self-Compassion Changes the Way We Experience Failure

If experience is part of the goal, can we really fail?

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Mistakes and failures don't have to define a person.
  • Radical self-compassion helps people reflect, learn, integrate, and grow.
  • If experience is part of the goal, then hard-earned lessons become perspective that can be carried forward.

Part of living means we will make mistakes and drop the ball from time to time. Things won't work out as planned, and we will come up short on something we worked really hard for. Sometimes we prepare as well as we can, give something everything we have, and still do not get the result we were hoping for. Perhaps the interview doesn't land, the project we poured ourselves into falls flat, or we lose a job because our position is eliminated. Or maybe we miss a deadline or snap at someone we care deeply about after a long day.

Some things that happen are completely outside our control. Life happens; sometimes we get knocked down, and it is not for us to understand all the moving parts. Other times, maybe we didn't bring our best energy or attitude; we were tired, distracted, or moving too quickly on autopilot, and we experience a failure. We also tend to make more mistakes when we're living in the zone of distress.

Whatever the cause, we can be quick to turn the event into a story about ourselves. We might tell ourselves things like: I'm a failure. I always drop the ball. Something is wrong with me. I should have known better.

Yet failures and mistakes are events, not characteristics.

Reframing Mistakes and Failure

A missed deadline is something that happened, not a description of your character. A plan that didn't work out is a circumstance, not a verdict on your ability. This shift in language matters, because when the story becomes about us rather than about what occurred, we stop looking at it clearly. The reality is that harsh self-criticism does not necessarily help us learn. It can feel productive, like we're holding ourselves accountable, but it tends to keep us stuck in shame, regret, and those "what if?" thoughts that play on repeat.

The Importance of Self-Compassion

The inner critic tends to get loudest at specific moments, like when we make a mistake, compare ourselves to others, or measure ourselves against where we thought we would be by now. A critic attacks identity, while a coach focuses on guidance, recovery, and the next right action.

What is fascinating from a neurological perspective is that the brain does not differentiate between our inner critic and criticism coming from someone else. That same visceral reaction happens when the voice is our own, except it is internal and often running in the background where we barely notice it. In one study, participants imagined responding to personal setbacks, mistakes, or failures either self-critically or with self-reassurance. Self-criticism engaged regions of the brain tied to error detection and behavioural inhibition, while self-reassurance engaged the regions we use to extend compassion to others (Longe et al., 2010).

Meeting a mistake with harsh judgment activates our threat system. When the brain is in this place and trying to protect us from shame, embarrassment, and vulnerability, there is very little room left for reflection. Meeting ourselves with understanding helps us feel emotionally safe and activates the parts of our brain that help us learn and grow. Across four experiments, participants who responded to a personal failure with self-compassion were more motivated to improve themselves (Breines & Chen, 2012).

We're not letting ourselves off the hook or abandoning accountability when we take an accepting approach. Self-compassion creates enough space for us to look honestly at what happened, take responsibility where we need to, and ask ourselves questions like:

  • What was outside my control? What was within it?
  • What can I learn from this?
  • What pattern keeps repeating?
  • What support was/is missing?
  • What can I do differently?

Those questions are much harder to answer from inside a threat response than they are from a place of steadiness. Dr. Kristin Neff's research on self-compassion shows that being gentle with ourselves promotes emotional well-being and hope (Neff, 2004). Radical self-compassion gives you the grace to say, "I'm human, and I made a mistake, but I am not the mistake."

Reflecting on Our Failures

Everywhere we turn are messages that can leave us feeling as though we are failing or falling behind. Few of us post about coming up short, so we carry shame around our setbacks while assuming everyone else is managing just fine. Yet I have never met a person who helped me level up, personally or professionally, who did not have bumps and hard lessons along the way. The tool I have found most useful for bridging that discomfort with perspective is what I call a failure journal.

My gentle invitation is that the next time something goes sideways or feels like a failure or disappointment, jot it down in a separate notebook. Then leave three or four blank lines underneath. A month or a quarter later, go back and fill in what happened because of it. Write what you learned, what it made possible, or what you know now that lets you make a different choice next time.

If Experience Is the Goal, You Cannot Fail

Our lives are a constellation of experiences, some good, some not so good, some that turned out better than we could have imagined, and some that still sting. If we define success strictly by outcome, it is very easy to feel like we have failed whenever the goal is not met. I believe that if we make experience part of the goal, we can't truly fail.

It is also worth remembering that you cannot come up short on something you never attempted. A setback means you were in it. It means you asked, you applied, you started, or you showed up for something that mattered enough to risk. The ones who never miss are often the people who never reach in the first place.

When we are willing to learn from something, we can never truly waste it, because there is always a lesson, a new perspective, a better strategy, or a deeper understanding to come upon. That is hard-earned wisdom that is ours to carry forward.

Final Thoughts

When we surrender self-judgment and meet ourselves with compassion, we unlock the opportunity to learn, to adapt, and eventually to share our hard-earned wisdom with others.

The next time something does not go the way you hoped, notice the first sentence you say to yourself and its tone. Then try offering yourself the same steadiness you would offer a friend who was standing where you are standing.

With each challenge, my wish would be that you gather wisdom, build perspective, and remember that you are enough, regardless of the outcome or misstep.

item.title: Study of a 117-Year-Old Woman Reveals Secrets of Longevity
item.description:
Aging

Study of a 117-Year-Old Woman Reveals Secrets of Longevity

Aging is inevitable, but resilience to age-related disease is key.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • A 117-year-old woman revealed that extreme longevity can occur despite systemic aging.
  • Genetic analysis found no single longevity gene explaining the woman's extraordinary lifespan.
  • The woman studied had a favorable lipid profile and a remarkably diverse gut microbiome.

Humans have always feared death, so one of our biggest dreams throughout history has been eternal life. Many cultures have told similar mythical stories about "fountains of youth" that heroes immersed themselves in to achieve immortality.

However, humans are intelligent and have since realized that escaping death is impossible. Therefore, we've begun to seek approaches to extend our lives as much as we can, and this search has continued into modern medicine. Thanks to medical advances, we have the longest lifespan among any human group in history.

But these achievements have still not been enough, and we've continued our efforts. The study of people who live longer than usual—especially beyond 100 years—has become a hot topic for curious scientists.

Lessons we learn from studying supercentenarians

A recent study of a 117-year-old supercentenarian woman revealed new insights into the aging process.

María Branyas Morera was born to Spanish parents in San Francisco on March 4, 1907. She was the oldest verified person in the world when she died. Before she died, scientists collected blood, urine, saliva, and stool samples from her and performed a series of highly advanced examinations (a high-throughput multiomics study) to determine the reason for this exceptional lifespan [1].

Perhaps scientists hoped to find a magical gene, protein, or biological pathway that explained her remarkable longevity; however, the results were more complicated. Maria did not have a specific gene or supernatural system; instead, she possessed a unique combination of aging and resilience to age-related diseases.

The scientists also looked carefully at her genome, hoping perhaps to find a genetic explanation for her extraordinary lifespan. Although they found many rare genetic variants related to immune function, metabolism, lipid regulation, and other biological processes, there was no single genetic change that could explain why she had lived to 117. Even one of the best-known longevity-related genes, FOXO3A, did not carry the variant usually associated with exceptional longevity in her genome. The genetic findings therefore suggested something important: extreme longevity may not depend on a single “longevity gene,” but on the combined effects of many small genetic and biological advantages.

Her telomeres—protective caps at the ends of each chromosome—were shorter compared to those of young people. Telomere length is the most essential factor in cellular aging. Additionally, Maria had aged immune cells, as expected from a 117-year-old person.

Some types of T-cells that often increase with aging were higher in her blood, but naïve T-cells were lower, a classic phenotype of aged immune cells. This contradicts several studies suggesting that a younger immune system promotes longevity. Despite her aged immune cells, she had never gotten cancer or deadly infectious diseases. However, she had a good autophagy pathway in comparison to older people. Autophagy is a cellular process in which cells eat some of their own defective or aged components. Therefore, these damaged organelles and compounds do not accumulate in the cells. It appears that this is important to rescue the cells from age-related failure.

Maria’s metabolic and microbiome profiles were remarkable

Interestingly, Maria had a very good lipid profile: very low levels of VLDL-C, triglycerides, saturated fatty acids, esterified cholesterol, and several hazardous lipid-risk markers, along with elevated HDL cholesterol. However, some metabolic markers also showed an age-related phenotype. Her inflammation markers show a favorable state. Moreover, the mitochondria in her immune cells, the cellular powerhouses, were healthier than expected for a 117-year-old person. The younger mitochondria may be associated with higher efficacy of autophagy that removes aged mitochondria.

A more fascinating finding of her stool sample was a greater abundance of the Bifidobacteriaceae family, including Bifidobacterium, within her gut microbiome. Some studies have shown that the composition of the gut microbiome correlates with better longevity, including Bifidobacterium [2]. However, since she regularly consumes about three servings of yogurt daily and follows a predominantly Mediterranean diet, it is difficult to isolate this bacterium as the direct cause of her long life. Still, her dietary habits and microbiome provide a significant clue.

In conclusion, although it is not scientifically valid to generalize findings from one person to the broader literature or public recommendations, several important lessons can be learned from these observations. Consistent with other studies, a better lipid profile, improved cellular health, and lower systemic inflammation appear to be key factors in promoting longevity, along with maintaining a healthy microbiome. However, the most significant insight from Maria’s experiments is that aging is an inevitable fate of the body, but some individuals exhibit resilience to age-related diseases. Longevity is related to a complex interplay of genetic, metabolic, microbial, and environmental factors. Other factors that are missed in this case are also important factors in the extension of lifespan; for example, the mental and psychological state. These factors have systemic outcomes that influence physical resilience to diseases.

item.title: When Cutting Off a Narcissistic Sibling Is Self-Protection
item.description:
Family Dynamics

When Cutting Off a Narcissistic Sibling Is Self-Protection

For some, distance may be the healthiest option.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • A study shows that 28 percent of adults experienced at least one episode of estrangement from a sibling.
  • Some siblings choose estrangement not as punishment, but as a boundary for protection after years of abuse.
  • Estrangement reduces harm, but also brings loneliness, stigma, complicated grief — and a chance to heal.

Many regard the sibling bond – the relationship that lasts longer than friendships or even the parent/child relationship – as unbreakable and essentially supportive. But recent research challenges that assumption, with 28 percent of adults in one study reporting at least one episode of estrangement from a sibling.

Often, those who distance themselves from a sibling are seen as impulsive, cold or unforgiving. Friends and relatives may judge them harshly, with statements like, “But he’s your brother,” or “How can you stop speaking to your only sister?” Even worse, some wonder, “What’s wrong with you that you can’t get along with your own family?”

Source: Timur-weber/pexels

But unacknowledged psychological forces may actually be driving some of the “28 percent” who chose to cut off. A long history of insults, gaslighting, competition, and family favoritism may exist. Often underpinning these relationships is a deep power imbalance, wherein one sibling absorbs the hurts and keeps showing up anyway.

In other words, a dominating sibling may have a pattern of entitlement, chronic envy, lack of empathy, blame-shifting, manipulation, and inability to tolerate anyone else’s needs. These are the qualities of people with Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD); however, clinicians view narcissism on a spectrum. Nearly everyone occasionally exhibits self-centered or egotistical behaviors.

A person with the full-blown disorder has rigid, severe traits that deeply disturb relationships in all areas of their lives. But some people have some narcissistic personality traits – not the full-blown disorder – and these repeated behaviors can incur deep emotional costs.

Identifying narcissistic personality traits

A shared childhood with a sibling who has narcissistic personality traits can turn rivalry into a lifelong competition for attention, status, parental approval, and inheritance. People with these traits may show the following behaviors and characteristics:

  • A sibling may have a need to always be right.
  • A conversation becomes a competition.
  • Any disagreement becomes proof of disloyalty.
  • The sibling’s success is minimized or hijacked.
  • Boundaries are perceived as insults.
  • A sibling may lack accountability and never apologize.
  • When pressed, a brother or sister quickly flips the conversation, so that their sibling ends up apologizing for having been hurt in the first place.

To tolerate these traits, a narcissistically abused sibling may learn to avoid certain topics, rehearse conversations and phone calls, soften good news to avoid triggering envy, and dread family gatherings. Relatives may make excuses, insisting, “That’s just how she is,” or “You know how he gets.” The request implied in these enabling statements is that one person should accommodate and carry the emotional burden for everyone else’s comfort.

Family dynamics that contribute to estrangement

Often, narcissistic sibling dynamics are deeply rooted in childhood. Parents may pit children against each other, especially when a father or mother is narcissistic. That parent who needs control, admiration, or loyalty may assign roles to each child: the golden child, the scapegoat, the invisible child, the responsible one. The favored sibling may feel entitled while the scapegoated sibling may carry shame. Both may compete for parental approval rather than learning to lovingly relate to each other.

One study of 202 young adults found that sibling warmth was linked with “low levels of narcissism,” while sibling conflict was linked with “high levels of narcissism." Narcissistic traits not only make someone hard to be around; they change the emotional climate, creating more conflict between siblings.

Another 2026 study in the Journal of Marriage and Family found that adult sibling estrangement may be rooted in patterns in the broader family system as every family member tries to cope with one child's toxic behavior. In other words, estrangement results from the family training everyone to protect the difficult sibling, and that sibling's behavior often becomes worse and worse.

A narcissistically abused sibling learns that forgiveness does not mean a family member has unlimited access, and love does not mean self-abandonment. In time, the hurt sibling may not only grieve the brother or sister they lost; they also may grieve the family that betrayed them by continuing to enable these behaviors.

Estrangement as protection

Ultimately, distance may not equal cruelty; rather, the decision to go no contact may have everything to do with self-protection. A sibling may have tried candid discussions, limited contact, mediation, forgiveness, humor, or accommodation. A sibling with narcissistic traits may respond to any perceived criticism with denial, counterattack, mockery, or pressure to “get over it” without any real accountability. In these situations, estrangement is not a punishment; it is a boundary.

For many people, walking away is the first time they have chosen emotional safety over the hope and fantasy that this time – somehow – the relationship will change. They refuse to be demeaned or controlled any longer.

A cutoff may be the healthiest response, even though it comes with grief. A 2025 qualitative study in Frontiers in Sociology described family exiting as emotionally complex, with people reporting both social gains and real costs. Estrangement may reduce exposure to harm, but it can also bring loneliness, stigma, and complicated grief.

But by cutting off, the hurt sibling also experiences a reclamation of self. Most siblings can’t diagnose a brother, sister, or parent from a distance. But they can identify the pattern and decide what relationship is possible. The narcissistically abused sibling refuses to keep paying for belonging by sacrificing his or her perceptions, dignity, and peace. At last, they see that they can feel safe and sorrowful at the same time.

The key question for narcissistically abused siblings may not be, “How can you stop speaking to your only brother?” It may be, “What were the costs of staying?” Ultimately, estrangement as protection may create the space for a sibling to begin to recover from a relentlessly damaging relationship.

item.title: Why Religious Patients Often Quit Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

Why Religious Patients Often Quit Therapy

Therapy's blind spot is costing patients real care.

Posted September 17, 2026

Picture this: A woman comes to therapy worn down by a difficult marriage, and when her therapist asks why she remains married, she answers that she made a promise before God. But this therapist sees it differently. To him, this woman is beholden to an irrational belief, and the solution is to build her capacity for self-advocacy. By the fourth session, she has stopped scheduling appointments. While perhaps nobody in that room was unkind, enough wires were crossed that the treatment couldn’t proceed.

Like the woman above, most religious patients don’t see faith-based counselors. Sometimes this is because they prefer someone outside of their community or because they’re seeking specialists on specific issues. But even when religious patients prefer therapies that aren’t focused on religion, they often still want a therapist who can discuss faith issues when they’re relevant (Kressel, 2026). Unfortunately, when these patients seek help, they often find providers who lack any competency with religious issues or even therapists who hold hostile or demeaning attitudes toward their beliefs.

Writing in Open Inquiry in Mental Health, psychologist Nina Silander argues that ruptures of this kind are increasingly common, predictable, and largely invisible to many psychotherapists. As Silander notes, a major cause of this trend is that mental health professionals are considerably less religious than the American public and therefore considerably less religious than the people whom they are supposed to treat. The size of that gap is easy to underestimate: Roughly three-quarters of Americans identify with a religious faith, while one survey found that only about a quarter of cognitive and behavioral therapists professed a certain belief in God (Kressel, 2026). Compounding the problem, graduate programs rarely treat knowledge of religion or spirituality as an essential clinical skill, and across 16 religious and spiritual competencies, between roughly half and 80% of surveyed psychologists reported little or no training (Vieten et al., 2016). The result is generations of therapists who feel unprepared to discuss religious topics, about a fifth of whom report never raising them at all (Kressel, 2026).

Silander traces this mismatch back to the field’s founding figures, many of whom were openly hostile to religion, with Freud treating it as a species of childhood neurosis and Albert Ellis regarding religious belief as irrational. While it’s true the field has softened since then (religiosity now appears in definitions of multicultural competency, and the APA maintains a division devoted to it), biases in research, training, and practice remain extensive (Kressel, 2026; Vieten et al., 2016).

The costs are enormous. Religious traditions offer a wealth of wisdom teachings, guidelines, and practices that have helped people lead fulfilling lives for millennia. Excluding these resources from treatment could severely limit what therapy accomplishes, especially in instances where patients are receptive to these interventions. And if a patient’s struggles involve a spiritual component, a therapist’s inability to discuss those topics could undermine the work entirely.

Additionally, research has consistently shown that religious involvement has a protective impact on health (Koenig, 2012) and is associated with lower rates of depression, substance use, and mortality, with the strongest effects showing up among people actively involved in a community rather than nominally affiliated (Li, Okereke, et al., 2016; Li, Stampfer, et al., 2016; Chen, Kim, & VanderWeele, 2020). One large cohort study of American health care professionals found that weekly attendance at religious services predicted substantially lower rates of death from drugs, alcohol, and suicide (Chen, Koh, et al., 2020). Given these findings, shouldn’t all therapists be able to engage in religious topics in a clinically sophisticated way?

But the most worrisome element of this problem may be therapists’ lack of moral diversity, since the moral intuitions people actually live by range well beyond the concerns about harm and fairness that dominate secular professional culture (Haidt, 2008). Therapists are often trained to “affirm,” which can sometimes be a useful stance, but it leaves the clinician with little to offer on questions of character, obligation, or virtue. And patients raise questions of these sorts constantly. Silander’s worry is that, lacking a coherent vocabulary for such moral concepts, mental health professionals will replace them with the language of coping skills and self-care, converting a patient’s moral quandaries into questions of regulation.

In other words, therapists might be too focused on how a person feels to ask whether a person is living well. To combat this dilemma, Silander’s recommendations are modest and mostly procedural, including taking the existing competency guidelines for religious and spiritual diversity seriously, and treating a patient’s faith as a significant part of the case rather than as mere background.

These steps are so obvious, it’s hard to understand why they haven’t already occurred. When these steps do occur, they will hopefully open up a broader dialogue about religious-spiritual questions that have been neglected for too long. It could significantly improve care, and help therapists to treat one of the largest overlooked clinical populations in the country.

item.title: Change the Story to Change Your Reality
item.description:
OCD

Change the Story to Change Your Reality

Author Chloe Benjamin on the role of storytelling in mental health.

Posted September 17, 2026

The stories we tell ourselves can shape our reality, contributing to anxiety, depression, OCD, or other mental health challenges when those stories take a fearful or bleak turn. Here author Chloe Benjamin shares her own mental health journey, and the role storytelling has played in leading to self-awareness and healing.

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write your latest novel, Under Story.

Source: Penguin Random House/Used with permission

Chloe Benjamin: I’m not a scientist, but I often write about them! Science fascinates me from a philosophical perspective, as a way to muse about big, existential mysteries. Scientific disciplines have come so far—we can send a shuttle into space and treat cancer—and yet there are these enormous questions we still don’t know the answers to: what happens after death, or whether there is other life in the universe. On the other hand, I’m also interested in spirituality, intuition, and feeling as alternate ways of approaching the unknown. Under Story is my third novel, and all of them circle these themes in some way.

As for the specific inspiration behind Under Story, there were two initial threads. In 2020, I heard about ANITA, a neutrino experiment at Antarctica’s McMurdo base. ANITA had detected unexpected results, and an outside scientist suggested that perhaps those results were evidence of a speculative model known as a CPT-symmetric universe. In this model, the Big Bang created two universes: the one we know, and a second universe where properties like time are inverted. This was disproven as an explanation for the ANITA results, but it captured my imagination.

At the same time, I was interested in exploring marriage. My second novel, The Immortalists, followed four different characters, and while there were some romantic relationships, that wasn’t its focus. By now, I’ve been married for many years, and I think long-term partnership can feel like a world of its own, both mundane and profound. I knew there needed to be a sense of tension for the sake of momentum, which is why I settled on the idea of a couple that is divorced by the time the book opens.

Q: What role does acceptance play in Laurel’s story? How does she ultimately find a way forward from her grief?

Chloe Benjamin: I think that on the face of it, Under Story might seem like a book about a couple who go back in time to fix a mistake. But in fact, as you say, I see it as being more about acceptance of what I call “the both of it”—the fact that life entails tragedy as well as joy no matter what.

Hopefully, over time, we find some degree of acceptance around that; otherwise, we live with even more anguish and resistance. But it’s very difficult. None of us choose to come into the world, and once we do, we have to cope with its challenges, from uncertainty about our futures to the inevitable loss of loved ones. I write about these things not because I have found acceptance, but because I’m trying to. And I love life—I love living, which is what makes the stakes feel so high.

Q: What role does psychology play in your work?

Chloe Benjamin: I think I’m a writer largely because I’m fascinated by other people—what their lives are like, how their minds work, how they go on despite hardship. If I hadn’t been an English major in college, I would have focused on psychology. After I finished my MFA in Creative Writing, while I was working on my first two novels, I worked in administrative positions in social services.

One of the ways that psychology and writing intersect for me is my interest in the power of story: how the stories we tell ourselves shape our realities. The Immortalists follows four siblings who go to see a fortuneteller, a woman who claims to be able to tell anyone their date of death; the novel then follows each sibling over the course of their lives to look at whether the prophecies come true and why. I was less interested in whether or not the fortune teller is truly psychic than in the power of the mind to influence the future. What is the difference between a prophecy and a self-fulfilling prophecy? Where is the line between story and history? I think of fiction and reality not as opposites but as two forces in a symbiotic, evolving relationship.

"Under Story" author Chloe Benjamin shares her own mental health journey and the role storytelling plays in psychology.
Source: David Enloe/Used with permission

I’ve observed the power of the mind in my own life as well. I have OCD, which is so much about fear, uncertainty, and storytelling. One of the siblings in The Immortalists has OCD, and after I wrote her character, I finally sought treatment myself; exposure therapy was transformative. I’ve also experienced chronic migraines, and after trying procedures and medications for years, I was transformed by brain-based approaches to chronic pain. Mind-body approaches like these see chronic pain as a physical response to psychological associations, the same way someone might get an upset stomach when nervous. In fact, MRI studies have found that in the brain, chronic pain is linked to learning and memory. But those links can be unlearned; the neural pathways can be retrained. If you change the story, your reality can change, too.

In Under Story, I wanted to explore consciousness. I think of consciousness as being, in part, the story of the relationship we have with ourselves. There is an internal dialogue, a conversation, that accompanies us all our lives. I was also really interested in exploring nonhuman sentience or consciousness. We humans tend to think of ourselves at the top of the hierarchy, but there is so much that we can learn from other organisms. I felt very tenderized while writing this book; the more you appreciate a pig or a tree, the more unbearable the thought of their suffering becomes.

Q: What do you hope readers take away from spending time with Under Story?

Chloe Benjamin: If I can help people to feel more wonder and care for all forms of life—or if they feel inspired to fight for the importance of physical experience and connection in an increasingly disconnected, virtual world—nothing would mean more to me.

item.title: The Loneliness of Being Unable to Forgive
item.description:
Forgiveness

The Loneliness of Being Unable to Forgive

How forgiveness can free us from resentment and help us reconnect.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Resentment is the opposite of forgiveness. Resentment is to feel anger again until we become paralyzed.
  • The person we cannot forgive is unlikely the one who becomes lonely. That person is us.
  • Forgiveness frees us up to trust again—just not necessarily the person we need to forgive.

Resentment is peaking these days. It’s become almost impossible to escape, as it’s highly visible to all of us, especially in political arenas all over the world.

Given that political polarization is now—in the United States at least, as I document in another post—at its highest level since the Civil War, it is safe to say that resentment is experiencing unprecedented popularity and becoming one of the most common emotions of our current generation.

Two Opposites

Resentment is the opposite of forgiveness. A word derived from the Latin roots re (again) and sentire (to feel), resentment is to feel anger again and again until you become paralyzed.

“Resentment is like drinking poison,” said the fourth-century theologian Saint Augustine, “and waiting for the other person to die.”

A recent Pew Research Center survey reveals that the percentage of Americans who view the Republican or Democratic party unfavorably is remarkably similar (58 vs 59 percent, respectively). Political polarization shaped by ideological divides occupies center stage, a stage in which the actors who foment outrage, vitriol, and an unwillingness to let go of age-old rivalries are constantly rewarded. A Cambridge University study, for instance, found that negative, hostile messages attacking an outgroup are twice as frequently shared or retweeted as messages toward one’s ingroup.

Yet these perennial enmities that have come to define bipartisanship may not even be the issue anymore. A new Pew Research Center political typology enumerates how Americans are divided into nine distinct factions with competing identities and values.

The Deeper Problem Is Not at the Polls

The deeper problem may not be political, but personal. Whether the person we cannot forgive is a former intimate partner, parent, coworker—or someone on the seemingly opposite side of the political aisle—the emotional root cause is stunningly similar: We make the same decision daily to continue reexperiencing an emotional injury and permitting the person whom we blame for hurting us to occupy our mental space in the present.

In my work as a leadership professor and leadership and life coach with CEOs, senior leaders, and individuals, I have discovered that the problems someone is experiencing at home or in the office can always—always—be traced back to someone from their past whom they judged and could never forgive. Further, the person we cannot forgive is unlikely to be the one who becomes lonely.

That person is us.

Forgiveness helps us feel less alone and more connected.
Source: Gus Moretta / Unsplash

What Forgiveness Does for You

A misunderstanding about forgiveness is that it is primarily something you do for other people. While forgiveness does benefit others, it is first and foremost for your own benefit.

One study revealed that Catholics and Protestants in Northern Ireland who lost a family member to violence and were able to forgive the murderer experienced a 40 percent decrease in depression. Another study by the psychologist Loren Toussaint that tracked 332 adults for five weeks found that forgiveness leads to better mental health and reduced stress. People who are forgiving have also been found to experience less loneliness, anger, and depression, more empathy toward others, and more closeness in their relationships.

As children, we’re often told by adults—generally with good intentions—to “forgive and forget.” To forget, however, may not be the best idea. If you fall into a ditch, the last thing you want to do is forget the location of the ditch. Such a strategy may result in your falling in again.

To Forgive Does Not Mean to Trust

Forgiveness, in fact, does not necessarily lead to a continued relationship. In many cases, forgiveness enables you to detach yourself from the relationship, not only physically but also emotionally and psychologically. Importantly, while trust binds, forgiveness releases. While forgiveness is needed for personal development, trust is needed for relational development.

Trust is not necessarily an evolutionary adaptive behavior, as it can lead to more harmful behavior from the other person. A man can apologize to his wife for an affair, for example, regain her trust, and then continue to cheat on her afterward.

While trusting a specific person whom you feel has harmed you is not necessary for your evolution as a human being, forgiving them is. Forgiveness is one of your most critical attributes because until you let go of your suffering, you don’t let it recede from the present and into the past.

Transcending Loneliness Through Forgiveness

Why is forgiveness so important, then? Because when you do not forgive, you remain “interpersonally stuck.” Meaning? You aren’t able to freely enter into other relationships and trust another person again.

Forgiveness creates space for relationships to thrive again.
Source: Christian Bowen / Unsplash

In other words, forgiveness frees you up to trust again—just not necessarily the person you need to forgive. Forgiveness becomes a lubricant that helps relationships launch and flourish. In your case, this could be the relationship with the person you need to forgive or a completely different relationship.

This means that, counterintuitively, you must forgive an interaction partner from the past to either welcome them back or to invite a new interaction partner onto your stage—whether as a friend, intimate partner, or even as a work colleague. Either way, no forgiveness means no one else on your stage—the entry point for loneliness.

While “Once bitten, twice shy” is true for most of us, “Once unable to forgive, twice unable to socially engage” is, unfortunately, also true.

Give forgiveness a try, and you will observe how both old and new relationships evolve around you and, if you are fortunate, thrive again.

item.title: Take Your Perfectionism and *Shove It*
item.description:
Perfectionism

Take Your Perfectionism and *Shove It*

You're going to make mistakes anyway because you're human.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • Perfectionism increases anxiety but rarely improves actual performance.
  • Research links rising perfectionism in youth to helicopter and intrusive parenting.
  • Letting go of perfectionism leads to more enjoyment and relaxed relationships.

As a recovering perfectionist, it took me a long time to learn the most important lesson: Perfectionism belongs in your rearview mirror. You're going to make mistakes anyway because you're human. Perfectionism doesn't stop that. It just raises the stakes on the consequences—mostly internal ones—while doing almost nothing for your actual performance. You just feel worse afterward.

Why Perfectionism Is on the Rise

I’m not alone in this. Research shows perfectionism is rising (Curran & Hill, 2017), especially among young people, and the leading theories mostly point a finger at parents—helicopter parents (Segrin et al., 2020) and intrusive parents (Hong et al., 2016). Progress, I suppose, over the Freudians, who just blamed the mother.

Parents can't win this one. But let's be honest, the way my grandmother was: "You can blame your parents for most things until you're 40. After that, you only have yourself to blame." Most of my family blamed her for plenty, because she was a strong woman in an era that didn't easily forgive that. I'd like to set the record a little straighter here, in her honor.

Back to perfectionism itself. We tell ourselves the trait pushes us to work harder and get things right, and that's a good thing. That's called relentlessness. We tell ourselves that if we want something done right, we have to do it ourselves. That's called micromanaging. And, most damningly, we tell ourselves we're never quite good enough to accomplish what we want to accomplish. In the long run, that's called despair.

All of that makes us harder to live with—tougher on ourselves, tougher on everyone around us, and less forgiving of the results. None of it actually helps. It just makes the race harder to run. Let's agree to stop.

Perfectionism is especially dangerous for leaders and keynote speakers, because the fear of making a visible mistake is perfectionism's cruelest form. There's something about standing in front of a thousand pairs of eyes that turns an ordinary brain lapse into a catastrophe.

Here's the trick I've learned for those moments: Don't carry the error alone. Hand it to the audience. Say, "I just lost my train of thought—does anyone remember what I was talking about?" It's remarkable to watch a room come to a speaker's rescue. They want you to succeed as much as you do. And you can relax, knowing that you don't have to know everything.

What Happened When I Let Go of Perfectionism

A few weeks ago, I took a short vacation and made a conscious decision to leave my perfectionism at home. I resolved not to get defensive, to own my mistakes, and to laugh instead of grimace.

How'd I do? Not perfectly—which, fittingly, was the point. Before the vacation had even started, construction at Logan Airport sent me circling the terminal a couple of times before I found my way into my usual parking spot. We still made it in plenty of time, and everyone in the car relaxed into the trip faster than they would have otherwise. I discovered that the new, relaxed "me" was more fun to be around. Here’s to my new motto: Imperfectionism forever!

item.title: Why You Think No One Likes You
item.description:
Self-Esteem

Why You Think No One Likes You

Our self-esteem is like our theory of self—whatever we think about, we see more of.

Posted September 17, 2026

Key points
  • If we struggle with self-esteem, praise, blessings, and loving relationships can make us feel worse.
  • We tend to underestimate how much people like us, a phenomenon called the liking gap.
  • Memories don’t just record the past; they predict the future.

Through writing my first book, Platonic, on making friends, I had my "one that got away" of psychology theories—self-verification theory. It suggests that we seek out people who see us like we see ourselves. This is true even if we see ourselves negatively. For example, there is fascinating research showing that if you see yourself negatively, you are less committed to spouses who treat you more positively. You actually prefer to interact with people who view you more negatively. When people give you positive feedback, your blood pressure spikes. Research has even found that the more positive events happen to you, the worse your physical health becomes. And you don’t even like praise coming from yourself. When people with low self-esteem repeated “I am lovable” at the sound of a beep, they felt worse afterward

It turns out that if we struggle with self-esteem, the very things we think would make us feel better about ourselves—praise, blessings, loving relationships—only make us feel worse.

What is going on here? This question powered a lot of my research for my new book, Worth: The New Science of Self-Esteem and Secure Attachment, and what I found was this: You can think of your self-esteem as a theory of self. If you see yourself positively, you think others will accept you, and if you see yourself negatively, your theory is that others will reject you.

The Liking Gap: Underestimating How Much Others Appreciate Us

This theory isn’t necessarily true, however. Often, people like people with low self-esteem much more than they think. For example, one study found that we tend to underestimate how much people like us, a phenomenon called the liking gap. The liking gap was even more pronounced for particularly self-critical people. How people thought their romantic partner viewed them, another study found, reflected less about how their romantic partner actually viewed them and more about how they viewed themselves.

Why would we develop this kind of theory if it often leads us astray? Robin Carhart-Harris, a professor in the Department of Neurology at the University of California, San Francisco, thinks that when we are hurt, life stops seeming predictable–anything bad can happen anytime–which is its own kind of pain. Craving certainty, our brain cements a story of ourselves (like "I’m bad") and others ("People will reject me"). Some semblance of certainty returns to us. Having even a negative theory of self protects us because we know what to expect. Rejection won’t surprise us; we’ll be prepared.

How Memories Shape Self-Esteem and Expectations of Rejection

This theory is developed from our memories. As researchers who study memory put it, “memory is considered to be a database for self-esteem.” You have memories of rejection, bullying, neglect, or even abuse, and memories don’t just record the past; they predict the future. A part of you thinks the rejection will happen again. That’s why staying insecure is adaptive.

If you already feel low, you won’t have as far to fall when the rejection eventually reoccurs.

This idea that self-esteem is a “theory of self” that rejects any evidence to the contrary is why it is so important to work on our worth. Without doing so, we can find our dream job and still feel like a failure, or the perfect relationship and still feel unloved. The beauties of life slip off of us. Unworthiness is an inability to process love.

If our unworthiness is rooted in the past, it may seem like we are hopeless. But we are not. We can change the past, or at least how it lives within us.
